And the election results could shape the federal housing agenda, plus local zoning and property taxes in several states. But whoever wins on Tuesday, come Wednesday morning, all of those political ads will finally be over. And that’s something we’ll all be happy about. I’m Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, sitting in for chief economist Danielle Hale . Let’s get into the Weekly Housing Outlook . Featured Report This week’s featured report is a two-for-one. Each quarter, we partner with The Wall Street Journal to find the top-ranked housing markets in America, covering the overall market and the luxury tier. Since summer, a lot has changed. Mortgage rates climbed from around 6.4% in July to over 7% by the end of September. Let’s see how those tougher conditions shaped the rankings. Senior economist Hannah Jones ranked the 200 largest metros on housing market conditions, local economies, and livability. Whenever mortgage rates climb, we start talking about refuge markets again. Those are places where each dollar goes further, so buyers head there when affordability takes a hit. And this quarter’s top-10 list is basically a map of refuge markets. Half are in the Great Lakes states, including Appleton, Wisconsin, South Bend, Indiana and Canton, OH. What a season for Wisconsin by the way. The Brewers win the World Series and Appleton takes the number one spot. The other half of the top 10 are smaller metros near pricier ones, like Lancaster and Reading outside of Philadelphia, or Manchester, New Hampshire, a short drive from Boston. These markets are all about relative bargains. In Canton, Ohio, for example, the typical monthly payment runs a third below the national average. But people will pay for value, and the secret is getting out. Asking prices across the top-20 are up 1.1% over the past year, while prices nationally are down. Senior economist Anthony Smith ran the same exercise for 60 luxury markets , and those buyers are chasing value too. Lifestyle markets that led earlier this year, like Boulder and San Jose, fell out of the top 10 in the fall. And St. Louis meanwhile grabbed the headlines, jumping from number 12 to number 1. Luxury starts around $670,000 there, versus $1.2 million nationally. So a national luxury budget would land you in the top 5% of St. Louis listings. Two metros made both the overall and luxury lists: Portland, Maine, and Bridgeport, Connecticut. I guess everyone really does love New England in the fall. The Week Ahead: Now, to the week ahead. It starts light, with Monday clear and all eyes on Election Day Tuesday, before the research reports and market indicators kick into gear. Wednesday brings our October monthly housing trends report, written by yours truly. I’ll take a look at whether elevated mortgage rates caused buyers or sellers to pull back more, as well as what happened to inventory, asking prices, and contract signings. As we await October’s data, let’s take a look back at the September snapshot, which showed a housing market softening under the weight of rising mortgage rates. Median list prices fell, while inventory and price cuts rose. I expect more of the same from the October data, when mortgage rates hit their highest levels since 2023. Speaking of mortgage rates, Thursday brings another Freddie Mac reading and commentary from senior economist Hannah Jones , alongside the Realtor.com weekly data update. It’s too early to call the direction of rates this week. But I’ll be watching the bond market, especially the 10-year yield, for any reaction to the midterms, new developments in the Middle East, and any Fed signals about a December hike. Rates matter locally too. For buyers in Phoenix, Tucson, Raleigh, Charlotte, and Louisville November 1st through 7th is your best time to buy . If rates ease for a third week in a row, buyers there and elsewhere could have more purchasing power than a month ago, more homes to choose from than a year ago, and fewer buyers to compete with. That’s a winning combination heading into the slow season. One final indicator: I’ll be up bright and early Friday morning to track the latest labor market data, which covers October unemployment and job growth. September was disappointing but not a disaster, adding just 29,000 jobs while unemployment rose to 4.2%. We expect the low-hire, low-fire labor market to continue, which keeps the Fed focused on inflation ahead of its December meeting. The Weekly Review: Now let’s look back at last week. And it was a busy one! Starting with what happened, or didn’t, at the Fed. As expected, the FOMC held its policy rate steady last Wednesday. items.description: Luxury Cut: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking By Anthony Smith Oct 29, 2026 The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking St Louis Downtown and Arch – SeanPavonePhoto/Adobe Stock St. Louis Returns to the Top St. Louis has made its way back to the top spot this quarter in the Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking. The top 5 rounds out with Charlottesville, VA; Portland, ME; Bridgeport, CT; and Pittsfield, MA, which took the top spot last quarter. Common themes across the top-ranked markets include low climate risk, lower unemployment rates, and higher levels of buyer demand. Each quarter, Realtor.com and the Wall Street Journal team up to identify the highest-performing and most attractive metro areas for luxury home purchases. We score 60 different luxury housing markets across the country in categories that include supply and demand strength, economic health, and quality of life. This fall’s ranking points to a return to fundamentals: markets with active buyer demand, homes that sell at a steady pace, and low exposure to climate risk moved to the front of the pack, while several lifestyle-driven markets that led earlier this year slipped out of the top 10. Highlights St. Louis climbs from No. 12 to No. 1 , reclaiming the top spot it last held in summer 2025, backed by the lowest cost of living in the ranking, strong buyer demand, and minimal climate risk. Four new entries joined the top 10 : St. Louis, Portland, ME (No. 3), Bridgeport, CT (No. 4), and Detroit (No. 6). Charlottesville, VA, reaches No. 2 , its highest placement yet, extending its run to six straight quarters in the top 10. Four markets exited the top 10 . Boulder, CO, fell from No. 2 to No. 15. San Jose, CA, dropped from No. 3 to No. 37. Santa Fe, NM, slipped from No. 4 to No. 16, and Santa Barbara, CA, moved from No. 10 to No. 17. Beyond the lower cost of living, the metro also has strong demand and low climate risk. The Midwest market is not often thought of when it comes to luxury, but it has many compelling draws compared to the higher price tags and elevated climate risk that accompany many coastal markets. The starting point for luxury in the St. Louis metro is just over $670,000 as of September, well below the national benchmark of roughly $1.2 million. In fact, a buyer at that national threshold would already be shopping in the top 5% of St. Louis listings, where the 95th percentile starts just under $900,000. Despite the lower price points, million dollar homes typically spend 59 days on the market compared to the 74 days at the national level. Only 3.7% of St. Louis listings are million-dollar homes, while the national share comes in at 12.5%. St. Louis also offers more for your money in the $1 million to $2 million price tier. The median home at that price point in the metro measures 4,430 square feet, compared to 3,016 square feet for the same price tier nationally. It has placed in the top 10 for six straight quarters, and this quarter’s No. 2 spot is its highest ranking yet. Some of its top attributes are low unemployment (3.1%), a cost of living below the national average and well below traditional coastal metros, and low climate risk. Luxury buyers in Charlottesville are also seeing more choice. The 90th percentile listing price sits at $1,360,000 as of September, down 5.9% year over year, while the number of million-dollar listings is up 14.6% from a year ago. items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Orange County Multifamily Market Report hereHighlightsConditions in the Orange County multifamily market remained stable in the third quarter, with vacancy flat while rents ticked higher.The vacancy rate held steady at 4.6% for the third consecutive quarter and is 20 basis points higher year over year.Combined asking rents for all classes, vintages, and locations of multifamily in Orange County increased 0.2% during the third quarter to $2,670 per month. Year over year, asking rents are up 0.6%. Year to date, multifamily investment sales activity is outpacing 2025, while the median sale price has increased nearly 20% to $365,200 per unit. The average cap rate across all property classes is 5.0%.Orange County multifamily market overviewProperty fundamentals in the Orange County multifamily market were little changed in the third quarter, with rents remaining near previous levels and vacancy holding steady. Deliveries remain elevated compared with last year, though the pace of completions slowed. This deceleration in supply growth occurred at the same time as a decline in absorption in recent months, keeping the vacancy rate flat for the third quarter in a row. Rent trends have been mixed in recent periods. While rents declined in several submarkets, the largest decreases occurred in Santa Ana and Anaheim, which had recently been among the strongest areas for rent growth. The recent decline appears to be more of a correction following outsized gains than evidence of a broader pullback in achievable rents.Multifamily investment activity has increased this year, with the market on pace to record its highest transaction count since 2022. Median pricing is also up from last year, although trends have varied by property class. Class A properties are trading at a median price of $425,500 per unit, down 7% from last year, while Class C pricing has increased 32% to $325,900 per unit. Class C assets have accounted for roughly two-thirds of all transactions this year, while only one Class B property has changed hands. More than half of all transactions have occurred in Anaheim, while Garden Grove has accounted for approximately one-quarter of total activity. Anaheim sales have been particularly concentrated, with every transaction occurring within a five-mile radius. Cap rates are generally ranging from the mid-4% to mid-5% range depending on property class and vintage.Employment:Employment increased by 6,300 jobs year over year. Employment increased by 6,300 jobs year over year, a 0.4% gain.The leisure and hospitality sector remained one of Orange County’s fastest-growing industries. Employment in this sector increased 2.1% year over year, with 5,100 new positions filled.The retail trade sector also posted stronger growth than has been typical in recent years. In the past 12 months, total employment in this sector increased 0.9%, with the addition of 1,300 jobs.Forecast: The current pace of employment growth is forecast to continue throughout the remaining months of the year. In 2026, total employment in Orange County is expected to rise 0.5% with the addition of roughly 8,400 jobs.Development and permitting:The construction pipeline spiked in recent months. Image The pace of deliveries in Orange County slowed during the third quarter, though year-to-date completions have already surpassed the 2025 total. Roughly 3,200 units have been delivered in 2026, more than double the amount recorded during the same period last year.The construction pipeline spiked in recent months, with projects totaling nearly 4,000 units breaking ground in the past three months. There are now nearly 7,400 units underway, up 16% from one year ago. Multifamily permitting slowed during the third quarter, though strong activity earlier in the year has kept year-to-date totals elevated. Through the first nine months of 2026, permits were issued for more than 2,500 units, roughly 50% above the same period last year. Forecast: Completion dates have been pushed back on a few properties, reducing the number of units that are expected to be delivered this year. In 2026, approximately 4,000 units are forecast to come online, up from nearly 2,200 units delivered in 2025. Vacancy:Vacancy went unchanged for the third consecutive quarter. Image The vacancy rate in Orange County was unchanged for the third consecutive quarter, remaining at 4.6%. Year over year, vacancy is 20 basis points higher.The city of Anaheim continued to be one of the best areas for vacancy performance in Orange County. The vacancy rate is forecast to reach 4.8% by year-end, up 20 basis points from one year ago.Rents:Mission Viejo has the strongest rent growth. items.title: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter
items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. Report Methodology ATTOM analyzed county tax assessor data for over 105.1 million residential properties for vacancy, broken down by foreclosure status and owner-occupancy status in the fourth quarter of 2026. items.title: Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens
items.description: Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens November 2, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private residential construction spending decreased in September 2026 driven by a steep decline in improvement (remodeling) spending. According to the latest construction spending data from the U.S. Census Bureau, private residential construction spending came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $848.8 billion in September, down 5.5% from the revised August estimates and lower by 8.9% from last year. The decrease in spending was primarily due to a sharp decline in improvement (remodeling) spending, which declined 13.0%. Over the year, remodeling spending was down 18.0%. Both spending on single-family and multifamily construction were unchanged from August but were down by 2.4% and 0.2% from a year ago, respectively. The decline in single-family construction spending is consistent with weak builder sentiment reflected in the NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) , amid rising interest rates, energy and material costs. The NAHB construction spending index shown in the graph below illustrates how spending on single-family construction has slowed since early 2024, reflecting the impacts of elevated interest rates and ongoing uncertainty over building material tariffs. Multifamily construction spending growth has also slowed down after the peak in June 2023, with the index largely plateauing since late 2024. In contrast, improvement spending has been on an upward trend since 2023, supported in part by the aging housing stock and sustained demand for renovation . However, the latest data is consistent with a 2026 soft patch for remodeling. Private nonresidential construction spending continued its upward trend. September’s spending rose 1.1% to a SAAR of $790.6 billion, and is 2.3% higher compared to the previous year. Data center construction, a subcategory within office cons truction , remained strong with spending increasing 8.6% month-over-month and 90.3% year-over-year, due to buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom Published on November 2nd, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down. Last Week’s Highlights The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected. The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back. Upcoming Attractions It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027. Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data. Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis. items.title: A path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table
items.description: Housing demand has stabilized over the last two weeks as rates have fallen a tad, and we can finally see a clear path back to sub-7% mortgage rates . We survived the crazy month of October, when the 10-year had the potential to close above 5.35%, which would have created a backdrop of bond-escalation selling, sending mortgage rates above 8%. That didn’t happen, of course, as the 10-year yield held that key line! Not only has the 10-year yield now gone below 5% — with mortgage rates closer to 7% than 8% today — but what this month has shown us is that there’s a clear path for sub-7% mortgage rates. Just the move in the last two weeks has stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, so let’s take a look on this Halloween on what needs to happen to get rates lower. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week was Fed week, and even Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said tighter policy has created financial pain for some AI companies. The Federal Reserve has been talking more and more about AI being very inflationary for many weeks now, so naturally, when AI companies are having debt-financing issues, and some are missing on their numbers, the 10-year yield has gone lower even with elevated oil prices and economic data staying firm. However, imagine for a minute that the Iran conflict was over: oil would be trading between $67 and $82. Imagine that the trade war 2.0 doesn’t get worse and you have an AI slowdown; there’s your trinity for lower mortgage rates. Nothing too drastic, but definitely sub-7%, and we’ve all seen what mortgage demand can do when rates drop below 6.64%. So there’s a pathway to 7%, but there’s also a pathway for rates to stay above 7% if the AI story rebounds, the conflict doesn’t end, and the trade war continues. This, of course, would need the economic data to stay very positive, as it has recently. Since Sept. 10, a clear head-and-shoulders pattern has formed in the 10-year yield so what I said above can break that lower and get us sub-7% rates. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multi-year lows. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%, since mortgage rates would already be over 8% now if this were not the case. Not only that, it would have been impossible to get mortgage rates near 7% again without a much bigger move lower with the 10-year yield. That said, when the 10-year yield moves lower at times, spreads can widen after a big move up because their job is to compress volatility. Now, this does wear off over time, and we can head lower again. What you don’t want to see is the Fed suddenly changing course and starting a massive rate-hike cycle, or a credit event like the Silicon Valley Bank crisis. items.title: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity?
items.description: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity? Many owners face the challenge of bringing more money into their deal. Sometimes, the cost may outweigh the benefits. Published Oct. 30, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . These days, it feels like you can find a stat to support just about anything you want. Think inflation isn’t an issue? If you watch the Sunday political shows long enough, someone probably has numbers to support that notion. On the other side, there’s probably someone who can tell you that the third-quarter U.S. real gross domestic product growth of 3.4% is a mirage. Think Brian Schottenheimer isn’t getting enough out of the Dallas Cowboys? (Spoiler alert: he isn’t, despite this week's win.) The folks at Pro Football Focus probably have something to back those claims. The same is true in multifamily. Since I started covering this sector, the number of studies, surveys and indexes that fill my inbox each day seems to have quadrupled … at least. I delete most of these research projects or studies because much of this “research” is sent under the guise of pitching products. However, I do look at certain reports and even seek others out. As more loans face issues in the apartment industry, I recently went to CRED iQ’s website to get an idea of the size of the maturity wall. There I found something that caught my eye — an article saying nearly 33% of maturing apartment debt needs a cash infusion to refinance. At first blush, that number felt, well, kind of low, given everything that I’ve been reading about maturity walls and refinance risk. Reading further on the CRED iQ website, I learned that the firm resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028. Of that $136 billion in debt, 23% of the loans and 31% of the balance can’t refinance without an equity infusion of roughly $6.8 billion. The good news for apartment owners is that money is available to fill that gap. The bad news: It’s getting more expensive. Earlier this year, Maximiliane Leachman, vice chair of CBRE’s debt and structured finance group, told me refinancing is becoming harder for some borrowers. At one point, these lenders may have wanted 1% to 3% of the loan balance for an extension. Now, many could be looking for 10%. “We’re all waiting for the shoe to drop at the end of this year as those borrowers come back for the second time to that debt fund for another modification,” Leachman said. “It will be interesting to see how many of those go back.” But costs aren’t the only issues owners must weigh when deciding whether to bring additional capital into their deals. In a recent conversation, Michael Lynd, CEO of Kairoi Residential, raised another concern: whether refinancing is worth the cost to existing equity holders. “The question that I have when I look at a lot of these refinances is the cost of that refinance is not great for your existing equity,” Lynd said. “If rent growth doesn’t show up in that first six to nine months or a year, then you have a chance of further impairing the equity value that isn't in place.” Lynd thinks a lot of groups are making decisions that might not be in their investors’ best interests by holding on to properties rather than selling them because they don’t want a negative trade on their record. Alternatively, they may want to delay a sale to raise additional capital. “I see it happening all over the place,” Lynd said. “You can get a loan, but should you take that loan? Is that the best risk-adjusted decision for your equity?” If the answer is no and if the market doesn’t snap back, those firms might be doing their investors a disservice. Still, some owners may find data showing refinancing is the best option. And it could be. But just because you can find the data to say something doesn’t make it so. items.title: The Data Center Election That Matters Isn't In Congress
items.description: Data centers have become one of the nation’s defining political issues ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. As tech giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to build behemoth facilities and use vast amounts of power to support their artificial intelligence race, communities have pushed back. Candidates on the federal, state and local levels have responded to data center opposition by proposing stringent regulations on the industry — and by painting their opponents as data center supporters. This contentious issue could influence the control of Congress and reshape statehouses across the country. Bisnow/created with ChatGPT But for all the focus on data centers on the campaign trail, industry experts say the election’s actual impact on the development boom may be less widespread than the rhetoric would suggest. In Congress, even if a wave of anti-data center Democrats take control of both chambers, they would still struggle to pass significant legislation that could receive the signature of President Donald Trump , a vocal supporter of the industry. In many states, candidates on both sides of the aisle are supporting stricter data center rules — meaning the industry is in for a tougher road no matter who wins. But there are state-level races in the key digital infrastructure markets of Texas, Pennsylvania and Georgia where candidates have staked out different positions, and the election could determine how much data center development will be allowed to move forward. Just in those three states, Morgan Stanley estimates the planned development of 284 data centers totaling more than 33 gigawatts of capacity are at risk pending the results of these races. “I don't think at the federal level the policy is going to shift much,” MOCA Economics Chief Economist Brandon Michalski told Bisnow . “If we go to the state level, that shifts dramatically and could change the trajectory significantly.” The Battle For Capitol Hill From Ohio and Michigan to Wisconsin, Texas and Maine, data centers have emerged as a major campaign issue in high-profile House and Senate races ahead of this week’s midterms. Data centers are deeply unpopular , and congressional candidates from both parties have made proposals to rein in development or limit its impacts a core element of their campaigns as voters voice growing concerns over electricity costs, environmental impacts and the broader consequences of the AI data center boom. The trend is especially visible in political advertising . As of the beginning of October, House and Senate campaigns had spent more than $29M on ads mentioning data centers, almost always negatively, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Bisnow . Although opposition to data centers cuts across party lines, Democrats have more aggressively nationalized the issue, contrasting calls for oversight of the sector with the Trump administration’s support for accelerating AI infrastructure development. Prominent congressional Democrats have already proposed measures like a national data center moratorium and released an investigation arguing that hyperscalers aren’t paying their fair share of grid costs. Now, party leaders are signaling their intent to make more aggressive oversight of the industry a prominent part of their policy agenda following the midterms, particularly if the party gains control of one or both houses of Congress. Last week, the Senate’s top Democratic tax writer announced plans to pursue an additional excise tax on data centers while eliminating the industry’s ability to tap a range of existing tax benefits tied to depreciation, research spending, opportunity zones and REIT structures. Although Republicans have also pursued measures aimed at addressing voter concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices, GOP leaders have privately acknowledged that data centers have become a winning issue for Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned major technology and AI firms in August that Democrats were successfully making data centers the “centerpiece” of the Senate race in Ohio and that deteriorating public sentiment toward the industry was becoming a broader risk to Republican candidates specifically. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” the letter warned . The data center industry has taken notice of this partisan dynamic. AI infrastructure super PAC Leading the Future and connected groups have spent significantly more supporting Republicans than Democrats, according to Forbes , while hyperscalers and AI giants like OpenAI have reportedly ramped up lobbying in anticipation of more aggressive Democratic oversight of data center development and the AI trade. Investors and analysts focused on the data center industry have similarly warned that the potential for Democratic victories in the House and Senate poses a threat to the industry’s growth and would bring greater regulatory and political risk. “There will be congressional hearings. There will be investigations,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel , according to Reuters. “You never know where that stuff leads, and there can be negative headlines.” Yet despite the rhetoric and the flood of money pouring into congressional races, not everyone is convinced that even a Democratic sweep would materially change the federal regulatory environment for data centers. items.title: Interior Finishes: The Most Time-Consuming Stage of Single-family Construction
items.description: Interior Finishes: The Most Time-Consuming Stage of Single-family Construction November 2, 2026 Paul Emrath No Comments Interior finishes (drywall, interior doors, painting, cabinets, countertops, plumbing fixtures, flooring, etc.) take more time to complete—6.4 weeks, on average—than any other major stage of single-family construction, according to results from the latest NAHB/Well Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) survey. The October 2026 HMI survey asked builders how long it takes to complete each of the seven major stages of construction traditionally used in NAHB’s construction cost surveys . The survey covers the steps a builder typically takes after purchasing a finished lot in the leading case of a single-family detached home built for sale . After interior finishes, framing and major systems rough-ins (HVAC and plumbing/electrical other than fixtures) consume the most time: 3.7 weeks each. Final steps (landscaping, outdoor structures and clean-up) require 3.6 weeks, and exterior finishes (siding, roofing, windows & doors) require 3.4. The earliest stages of the construction process, site work and foundations, require the least amount of time—a little over two weeks each, on average. The most time-consuming stages of construction are also in general the costliest. In NAHB’s latest construction cost survey, for example, interior finishes account for over 24% of the builder’s construction costs, significantly more than any other stage of construction and roughly proportional to the amount of time that stage consumes in the overall construction process. Final steps, however, break this general rule by being the least expensive stage of construction but consuming a disproportionately large amount of construction time. The complete cost breakdown by stage of construction, along with a more detailed description of each stage, is available in Cost of Constructing a Home-2024 . In total, NAHB’s October 2026 HMI survey shows that it takes 25.3 weeks (about 5.8 months) to build the average single-family detached home, close to the average time of 6.1 months from start to completion reported by the Census Bureau for a single-family home built for sale in 2025. The Census estimates show that custom homes (e.g., contractor-built homes built one at a time on the home owner’s lot, and owner-built homes where the owner functions as the general contractor) take significantly more time to complete. Moreover, these numbers are averages, and it’s important to remember that the time it takes to build a particular home will vary based on geography and characteristics of the home and its builder. The Census Bureau’s time-to-completion estimate is based on a considerably larger and more intricately stratified sample than the one from NAHB. Hence, the Census estimate is the one you would use if you’re interested simply in total construction time for a single-family home. NAHB’s new 25.3-week time-to-completion estimate, however, has the obvious advantage of breaking down the time by stage of construction. The extra detail may be useful to a builder who wants to educate customers, decide when to purchase building materials, schedule inspections, or manage subcontractors. construction time , Housing Market Index (HMI) Prev Previous Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter Next Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens Next Leave a Reply Cancel reply Your email address will not be published. items.title: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter
items.description: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter October 30, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private fixed investment in student dormitories rose 2.6% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $3.8 billion. This gain marked a second consecutive quarterly increase, despite continued pressures from elevated interest rates. On a year-over-year basis, investments in dorms increased 1.1%. Private fixed investment in student housing experienced a surge after the Great Recession, as college enrollment increased from 17.2 million in 2006 to 20.4 million in 2011. However, during the pandemic, private fixed investment in student housing declined drastically from $4.4 billion (SAAR) in the last quarter of 2019 to $3.1 billion in the second quarter of 2021. According to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center , college enrollment fell by 3.6% in the fall of 2020 and by 3.1% in the fall of 2021. The latest preliminary data indicated that college enrollment held steady in fall 2026 compared with the previous year. Since the pandemic, private fixed investment in dorms has rebounded alongside a gradual recovery in college enrollments. Effective in-person learning requires college students to return to campuses, boosting the student housing sector. Still, demographic trends are reshaping the outlook for student housing. The U.S. faces slower growth in the college-age population as birth rates declined following the Great Recession. Furthermore, changing perceptions towards the value of a college degree as a guaranteed pathway to job security are all contributing to an “enrollment cliff”. According to the National Center for Education Statistics , total enrollment in postsecondary institutions is projected to only increase approximately 2% from 2026 to 2031, well below the 37% increase between 2000 and 2010. student housing Prev Previous Housing’s Share of the Economy Falls Again as It Continues to Face Headwinds Next Interior Finishes: The Most Time-Consuming Stage of Single-family Construction Next Leave a Reply Cancel reply Your email address will not be published. items.title: Rocket posts $709M profit in Q3 despite tougher mortgage market
items.description: Rocket Companies on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of $709 million, reversing a loss from a year ago as the Detroit-based mortgage lender expanded revenue and gained market share in purchase and refinance lending. The company reported net income of $709 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a net loss of $124 million a year earlier and a second-quarter 2026 net income of $229 million. Net total revenue nearly doubled year over year to $3.28 billion, up from $1.7 billion, while adjusted revenue rose to $2.57 billion, up from $1.87 billion. Adjusted net income fell to $419 million from $441 million in Q2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA declined to $748 million from Q2's $766 million. Mortgage production also slowed, with closed origination volume falling to $43.6 billion, down from $49.1 billion. The sequential decline in adjusted earnings came as mortgage production slowed from the second quarter, even as the company reported a slightly higher gain-on-sale margin. Rocket chief financial officer Brian Brown anticipated the slowdown during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call, saying he expected Q3 to be “smaller than the second,” a contraction not seen in the industry since 2022. He cited rates above 6.8% and rising inflation expectations as key challenges. “Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” CEO Varun Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage , and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.” During the company's earnings call on Thursday afternoon, Krishna addressed the broader market. "Here's the truth about tough markets: They don't lie," he said. "They strip everything down to what's real. Who has the capital to keep investing? Whose model works in any cycle? Who can win their clients back? And who can move fast when it counts? This quarter did all of this." Brown said during the call that the company estimates its purchase market share approached 6.5% in Q3 2026, up from 6.2% in Q2 2026. Its refinance share reached 15.5%, compared with 14.3% from April through June. Mortgage production and servicing Rocket closed $43.6 billion in mortgage originations in the third quarter, down from $49.1 billion in Q2. Net rate-lock volume fell to $40.4 billion from $47 billion over the same period. The company’s total gain-on-sale margin edged up to 2.54% from 2.48% in Q2. Excluding correspondent lending , Rocket closed $33.5 billion in mortgage volume during the third quarter. Direct-to-consumer lending accounted for $24.6 billion, while wholesale channel Rocket Pro generated $9 billion. The correspondent channel contributed $10.1 billion in closed volume. Rocket’s mortgage servicing portfolio remained steady at about $2 trillion in unpaid principal balance across 9.1 million loans. The company sold mortgage servicing rights tied to $23 billion in unpaid principal balance during Q3, generating $379 million in proceeds. That was down from $53 billion in MSR sales and $795 million in proceeds in Q2. Rocket retained subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the servicing rights sold in the third quarter, compared with nearly 80% in Q2. Total liquidity rose to $11.4 billion at the end of Q3, up from $11.2 billion at the end of the prior quarter. The figure includes $2.7 billion in cash, $2.5 billion in undrawn credit lines and $6.2 billion in available servicing-rights and advance lines. Rocket said its combined servicing portfolio following the Mr. Cooper integration continued to support borrower recapture, with the company reaching its highest recapture levels to date. During Q3, Rocket continued to expand its use of artificial intelligence and its partnerships with real estate companies. The company said it pulled credit on nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer loan volume before borrowers spoke with a loan officer, compared with none a year earlier. Digital mortgage applications accounted for more than 40% of retail refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of nondigital leads. AI voice technology handled 65% of inbound servicing calls, resolving more than half without human assistance. Rocket also reported growth in its real estate partnerships. Redfin visitors who clicked to begin a mortgage transaction increased 50% year over year, while Redfin’s contribution to Rocket’s refinance leads more than doubled in Q3. Listings tied to its Compass partnership reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in Q2. In September, Rocket Mortgage adopted VantageScore 4.0 as its preferred credit scoring model for eligible loans. The company said its testing indicated qualifying borrowers could save an average of $1,600 in closing costs. Rocket Pro launched Orbit in October , offering eligible purchase borrowers same-day conditional approval and a 12-business-day timeline to clear-to-close. The company also extended a Compass pricing credit through the end of 2026. The partnership had generated more than $3 billion in rate locks since February. Brown said that the company expects the market to weaken further as mortgage rates remain elevated and seasonal trends reduce activity. The company estimated purchase mortgage applications were down nearly 20% year over year, while refinance applications had fallen more than 50%. items.title: Open Real Estate gets a boost from independents — and an opening from MLSs
items.description: A week after Open Real Estate , a broker-led initiative to build a shared infrastructure for residential listing data, launched , the initiative announced that it has secured 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders across the country. Independent firms account for the majority of that backing, with 493 letters, or 59%, coming from independent brokerages, according to an announcement on Monday. Support spans single-office independents to some of the largest independent firms , including Atlanta Communities , Iron Valley Real Estate , LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America , all RealTrends Verified brokerages. The effort is designed as a national, shared data layer that connects brokerages, agents, multiple listing services and real estate portals. Founding organizations include AGNT Inc . (parent to eXp Realty and NextHome ), HomeServices of A m erica , Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group , all RealTrends Verified brokerages. “We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” the founding members of Open Real Estate said in a joint statement. MLS leaders signal willingness to collaborate Open Real Estate’s backers say the project is meant to complement, not replace, existing MLS organizations by expanding access to listing information for brokerages, agents and consumers. Several prominent MLS executives publicly welcomed collaboration with the initiative. “We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” Brian Donnellan, the president and CEO of Bright MLS and a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. Art Carter, CEO of California Regional MLS (CRMLS), added that the effort aligns with CRMLS’s long-running work to give brokers more flexibility in how they input and manage listing data. “Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform. It has been a long-term project of CRMLS to allow our brokers to have that ability,” Carter, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.” North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS) CEO Chris Carrillo framed Open Real Estate as part of a broader conversation about transparency and equal access to listings. “NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative and neutral marketplace that serves all broker participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” Carrillo said. And NorthstarMLS President and CEO Tim Dain emphasized that broker-driven projects can coexist with MLSs. “Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” Dain, also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.” The push for a shared listing data infrastructure comes as the industry adapts to rapid changes in how listings are distributed and displayed, ongoing antitrust scrutiny and shifting brokerage business models. Brokerages are looking for more direct control over how their listing data flows to MLSs, portals, internal systems and third-party tools. Open Real Estate’s founders position the initiative as a way to streamline listing distribution, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace, particularly as consumer expectations for transparent, real-time listing information continue to rise. items.title: Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home
items.description: Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home Published on October 30th, 2026 by Kynsay Hunt Redfin today launched Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America , a creative franchise on Redfin.com bringing America's history to life through the remarkable homes and people that helped shape the nation. The franchise invites everyone to explore iconic homes through immersive digital experiences and free public events, starting at Philadelphia’s Betsy Ross House on November 7. From today, Redfin is celebrating America's 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America. With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide. The series debuts with two properties: The Betsy Ross House in Philadelphia: A landmark associated with the creation of the American flag and the story of a pioneering craftswoman and entrepreneur whose work became part of the nation's identity. 1892 Bishop’s Palace in Galveston, Texas: A one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition. Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027. “America's story isn't just written in history books. It's written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.” The Betsy Ross House: A Home Woven into the American Story Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America's founding. The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades. The home's remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning. Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms. 1892 Bishop’s Palace: A Remarkable Gilded Age Home Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923. Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa. The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south. Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition. Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. items.title: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal
items.description: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal Although the mega-merger made 2026’s third quarter the highest on record, apartment values fell 4.6% year over year and 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3. Published Nov. 2, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google The Avalon at Palisades in Charlotte, North Carolina. AvalonBay Communities acquired the property before it became Vivmark. Permission granted by AvalonBay Communities Dive Brief: The third-quarter apartment sales landscape was very similar to August’s, with sluggish single-asset sales. Still, the merger of Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities drove deal volume up 139% year over year to $114.1 billion, according to a report that data firm MSCI Real Assets shared with Multifamily Dive. The RCA CPPI for apartments declined 4.6% YOY. It fell 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3, as pricing deteriorated over the past four months. The annualized decline in values in each quarter has outpaced the yearly drop. In contrast, the RCA US National All-Property CPP rose 0.9% YOY. Without the creation of Vivmark, sales would have fallen 7% YOY for the quarter and been flat so far for the first nine months of the year. However, with the deal, 2026’s third quarter was the largest on record, surpassing $90.4 billion in 2021 and $78.4 billion in 2022. It was the second-largest quarter on record, falling only behind Q4 2021, which tallied $167.1 billion in trades. Dive Insight: Prices usually follow transaction growth, with investors underwriting appreciation as they bid, according to MSCI. “Here, volume is rising while prices fall, which points to a single transaction rather than broader confidence in the apartment sector,” MSCI said in the report. The usual gauge of industry health, individual sales, dropped 12% YOY to $34.3 billion in Q3, marking the second straight quarter of decline. In the six major metros, individual sales were approximately flat at $11.8 billion, while they dropped 17% YOY to $22.5 billion in non-major cities. The Vivmark deal pushed up volume across various subtypes. Portfolio sales rose 19% YOY to $10.2 billion on the strength of the Vivmark deal, while mid- and high-rise transactions jumped 248% YOY to $70.2 billion. The market was hardly thriving before the 10-year Treasury began rising six months ago. But since then volumes have declined, and cap rates have risen. In Q1 2022, cap rates sat at 4.5%, according to MSCI’s hedonic rate calculation. Now they’re 140 basis points higher. While much of that movement came in early 2024, they climbed 20 bps over the last year to 5.9% in Q3. As the 10-year Treasury moved above 5% in Q3, owners say it has become difficult to project deals they’re underwriting . “The last 60 days have been difficult, and from our end makes it difficult to pin down where we think exit caps are going,” American South Capital Partners Executive Vice President Tyler Epps told Multifamily Dive. Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital, said that “cap rates have moved out since the September [Federal Reserve] meeting,” and sellers are slow to accept it. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser previously told Multifamily Dive. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.title: The Geo Group To Reopen 2,329-Bed Immigration Facility In Texas
items.description: The Geo Group expects $340M in annual revenues from two new U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility contracts, including one that will reopen a 2,329-bed immigration processing center in West Texas. Google Maps The Geo Group's Big Spring Complex in West Texas Big Spring, Texas, entered into a 10-year contract with ICE for the reactivation of the Big Spring Complex, which includes the 1,404-bed Flightline Facility and the 925-bed Cedar Hill Facility, Geo announced Monday . The Geo-owned facilities have been closed since 2021, after contracts with the U.S. Bureau of Prisons expired, according to NewsWest 9 . The Big Spring facility is expected to generate about $200M annually for Geo and is one of two contracts announced by the group in the past week. Geo also secured a 10-year contract to continue managing the 1,635-bed, Geo-owned Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, which is expected to generate about $140M in annual revenues for Geo. The company will provide security, maintenance and food services, as well as access to recreational amenities, medical care and transportation services, at both facilities. Geo has been used by the federal government to hold migrants for 40 years. Last month, the Department of Homeland Security paid Geo $950M for three Adelanto, California, facilities . This acquisition came as part of the government's strategy to buy facilities to detain and deport unauthorized immigrants. Geo and CoreCivic have been the primary sellers. After pivoting from warehouse acquisitions, DHS awarded contracts worth up to $7.3B to potentially build new immigrant detention facilities. DHS also agreed to pay CoreCivic and Geo $240M annually to reactivate defunct immigrant facilities. “We expect that our Big Spring Complex in Texas will play an important role in helping meet the need for increased federal immigration processing center bedspace,” Geo CEO George Zoley said in a statement. The number of immigrants in detention increased from 60,311 to 65,765 between April and July, according to Trac Immigration . There were 16,450 ICE detainees in Texas, the state where ICE relied on detention facilities to house the most people this year, according to data from July. items.title: Rocket warns 2027 mortgage market will be worse than expected
items.description: Rocket warns 2027 mortgage market will be worse than expected By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 29, 2026, 7:14 p.m. EDT 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Uncover how Rocket is bracing for a mortgage market downturn which defies industry forecasts. Expert Quote: "Today, based on our estimates, the same data points to a fourth-quarter market well below what industry forecasts indicate." — Brian Brown, President and CFO Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content Rocket marked four financial quarters of owning Mr. Cooper with its highest profit margins in five years, at a time when mortgage rates reached their highest levels since 2003. The quarter results were very good, both in terms of profit and production. But going forward, the mortgage environment will be tough, not just in the fourth quarter, but also throughout 2027, Rocket executives said on the earnings call. They were even more bearish than industry forecasts from the Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae. The fourth quarter normally is a low one production-wise for the industry and this one is being impacted at a time when mortgage rates are at levels not seen in two decades, said Brian Brown, Rocket Cos. president and chief financial officer. What the real time data is revealing about the fourth quarter "Last quarter, we told you our real-time data pointed to a third-quarter mortgage market that would be smaller than Q2, something the industry had not seen since 2022. That is exactly how the third quarter played out," Brown said. "Today, based on our estimates, the same data points to a fourth-quarter market well below what industry forecasts indicate." Rocket expects the overall refinance market to decline by almost half from the third quarter, which will push volume to "multi-decade lows," Brown warned. This guidance was weaker than BTIG's estimate, which analyst Douglas Harter attributed to Rocket's "more conservative outlook for market size." When it comes to 2027, CEO Varun Krishna did not mince words. "The reality is this may be the toughest mortgage market in more than 30 years, but let me just tell you, I like tough markets because when you're playing in this nosebleed territory, no one can really hide," he said in response to an analyst's question. "We've been calling for a smaller market than the industry forecast, and that's pretty much exactly what we've seen quarter after quarter after quarter," Krishna said. "When you look at 2027, you know the forecasts are below $2 trillion; we think it could actually be even smaller still." In this environment, the executives pointed out that Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance. What was Rocket's third quarter volume? Inclusive of the correspondent channel, Rocket produced $43.6 billion at a 254 basis point gain on sale margin. This compared with $49.1 billion at a 248 basis point margin. The volume was 3% lower than Harter's estimate. The miss was from the third party channels, as wholesale came in 5% under and correspondent 8% below BTIG. Rocket did not acquire Mr. Cooper until Oct. 1 of last year. It closed the Redfin transaction at the start of the third quarter of 2025. For the third quarter a year ago, Rocket did $32.4 billion at a 280 basis point margin. In the wholesale channel, "over 200 brokers have now activated with Rocket, that represents almost $12 billion in potential annualized volume," Krishna said. "So, four consecutive quarters of expanding margins, taking share and better economics. That's kind of the combination that we're solving for." In the current period, Brown said per channel margins are running similar to the third quarter. The company ended the quarter with a $2 trillion mortgage servicing portfolio. Rocket's MSR sales during the period totaled $23 billion, generating $379 million of cash proceeds. Furthermore, management noted it retained subservicing and recapture rights on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Rocket reports a GAAP profit The third quarter was the second consecutive quarter of GAAP profitability for Rocket, with net income of $709 million. This compared with net income of $34 million in the second quarter, and a loss of $124 million one year ago. When asked about competition, Krishna responded "I think the reality is the market is literally testing every single lender, and that's like a good news, bad news story. I think the good news is if you have a strong business model, guess what? It's going to shine through. But the bad news is if you have a flaw in your business model, it's going to get exposed." Earlier Brown noted in the past lenders have used pricing as a lever to drive volume in times of scarce originations. He is not seeing as much of it right now. On the call, they addressed the recapture opportunities, noting the home equity lending business is benefitting. Rocket also got 20% of its quarter's purchase volume from Redfin's agreement with Compass announced earlier this year. items.description: VantageScore president and CEO resigns amid credit score war By Colin McNamara Published November 02, 2026, 2:49 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Quote: "I am humbled by all that VantageScore has achieved during my tenure." – Silvio Tavares Supporting Data: VantageScore more than tripled its market presence during Tavares' tenure. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content Amid an escalating mortgage credit score war , VantageScore President and CEO Silvio Tavares is stepping down, the company announced Friday. VantageScore's board of directors appointed Anthony Hutchinson, who has led the company's public affairs and government relations efforts, to replace Tavares on an interim basis. The company denied requests for comment on the reasoning behind Tavares' resignation. "I am humbled by all that VantageScore has achieved during my tenure," Tavares said in a press release. "Together, we consistently delivered industry leading innovation and growth at a very high scale. Along the way VantageScore responsibly expanded access to credit so that millions more creditworthy Americans can achieve their American dream." During his five-year tenure, the company more than tripled its market presence and saw widespread adoption of its crediting-scoring model throughout the mortgage industry. VantageScore is positioned for continued growth and innovation, driving the use of more predictive, inclusive tri-bureau credit scoring models, the company said. Prior to his time at VantageScore, Tavares served as president and CEO of Digital Commerce Alliance, where he maintains a role as chairman of the board of directors, according to his LinkedIn. Hutchinson has more than 30 years of housing finance, public policy and industry leadership experience. He joined VantageScore four years ago after holding senior positions at Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae and the National Association of Realtors. As interim president and CEO, he will work closely with VantageScore's board and management team, helping to further advance its strategic priorities, according to the release. Tony Hutchinson, VantageScore interim president and CEO "VantageScore is helping lenders make more predictive, inclusive and informed decisions across the credit lifecycle," Hutchinson said in the release. "I look forward to working with the VantageScore management team and board of directors to build on our success and to drive continued innovation that opens up more financial opportunities for more consumers." VantageScore vs FICO VantageScore has been active this fall in its efforts to gain a larger share of the mortgage credit scoring market. TransUnion, one of the three credit bureaus that jointly owns VantageScore, announced in September the extension of its discounted 99-cent pricing for Vantage 4.0 through the end of 2028. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte also ordered Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to accept VS4, and major lenders, like Rocket Mortgage and Pennymac, adopted the model. Fair Issac Corp. responded two weeks ago with the launch of a flat fee initiative . The company will maintain its mortgage price for credit scores through its tri-merge resellers at $10 for "Preferred Program" members. The bundled deal includes both the classic FICO score and the newer 10T metric the government-sponsored enterprises plan to add alongside VS4. Fairway Home Mortgage, Movement Mortgage and Rate all reported Friday they committed to the package . items.title: Brookfield, CPP Complete $5.2B REIT Buyout, Pick Up U.S. Logistics Assets
items.description: Brookfield Asset Management and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board completed a $5.2B deal to take logistics operator LXP Industrial Trust off the New York Stock Exchange. Unsplash/Bernd Dittrich The two Canadian giants — BAM is the New York-based investment management arm of Toronto-based Brookfield Corp. — completed an all-cash deal to buy and delist the South Florida-based REIT and its 107-property portfolio across the Midwest and Sun Belt . Brookfield Real Estate CEO Lowell Baron said the deal for the 52M SF portfolio fit within the firm’s conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the U.S. industrial sector. The joint venture between Brookfield and CPP Investments paid $61.20 per share to delist LXP and take the company private, a 12.3% premium on LXP’s 30-day weighted average share price at the time of the offer. The deal, first announced in July , included a 40-day window in which LXP management could have sought a better buyout price. In June, management valued the then-108-property portfolio at $4.7B in a presentation to investors. The portfolio was 96.6% leased at the time with average in-place rents of $5.28 per SF. Nearly all of the portfolio was new, bulk distribution real estate. The REIT reported $49.5M in funds from operations in the second quarter , up $2.2M from the prior quarter and 5% year-over-year. It sold one property in the second quarter for $51M and acquired a 37-acre infill covered land investment in Phoenix for $103.2M. LXP also began development on two speculative projects in Columbus, Ohio. The REIT has a diversified tenant base. Its largest tenant is Amazon , which occupies 6.7% of its portfolio, and its top 10 tenants account for roughly a third of its occupancy. Its properties are spread across Arizona, Texas, Indiana, Ohio, Tennessee, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida. “With strong occupancy and exposure to key distribution markets, we believe LXP is well positioned to capture further value as logistics markets evolve, supporting attractive long-term returns for the CPP Fund,” Sophie van Oosterom , head of real estate at CPP Investments , said in a statement Monday. The U.S. industrial market has proven resilient even as developers created a glut of new construction during the pandemic. Absorption in the third quarter was at its highest rates since the start of 2023, and demand surpassed 70M for the second time in as many quarters, according to Cushman & Wakefield ’s third-quarter market report. National vacancy is at 6.8%, its lowest level since the end of 2024. items.title: UK Budget Risks Deterring Sovereign Wealth Funds From Real Estate
items.description: The budget is out, and the property industry has concerns. UK Chancellor John Healey avoided a bond-market shock with his “breathing space” budget , and the immediate financial-market reaction was reassuring. Gilt yields did not spike, avoiding an outcome that could have pushed financing costs up even further. However, investors were left waiting for measures capable of bringing borrowing costs down and stimulating new development. The budget also delivered limited progress on development viability, while business rates measures offered some relief to high street occupiers without delivering the structural reform sought by many property owners. But new proposed tax rules for sovereign investors, which threaten to make the UK less attractive to global property capital, caused a sharp intake of breath. Flickr/House of Commons Chancellor John Healey succeeded in placating bond markets, but the property sector raised concerns over sovereign taxes. The government has launched a consultation over its proposal to replace the largely noncodified sovereign immunity from direct taxation with a statutory regime from 1 January 2029. Certain UK property income and capital gains would become taxable, although the reforms include bespoke access to the real estate investment trust regime, with a 15% tax rate on qualifying property income distributions. State-operated overseas pension funds and certain investment management activities would remain exempt. The government claimed the reforms would improve transparency and provide greater certainty for sovereign investors, but many in the property industry worry it could weaken the UK's appeal to investors. “It’s a really unhelpful change,” Real Estate:UK Assistant Director of Finance Rachel Kelly said. She said the proposal introduces additional costs for a significant source of real estate investment while development viability is already under severe pressure. Sovereign wealth funds invested £6.2B in UK property from 2021 to 2024, according to a March report from BPF and CoStar . Although the proposed REIT arrangements and transitional provisions offer some flexibility, the new 15% rate would be a significant increase for qualifying sovereign investors accustomed to paying no tax. It also adds an onerous process. “In addition to the actual additional cost now of investing in the UK for those investors, there will be huge complexity in terms of having to restructure their investments, and there will be a lot of work for some to change how they're structured,” Kelly said. The implications extend beyond the funds themselves. Sovereign wealth funds frequently invest alongside other capital providers, meaning changes to their investment structures could affect co-investors and joint ventures too, Moorfield CEO Charles Ferguson-Davie said. He said the reforms risk sending the wrong signal. “There aren’t that many groups that will deploy over £500M, over a billion,” Ferguson-Davie said. “If they’re going to be less active as a result of having to pay tax, who’s going to step in and invest that money instead?” CBRE Investment Management is looking to understand the rules in more detail during the consultation, Director Alex Lund said. But he expressed optimism that the policy won’t decimate investment. “For any market looking to attract overseas capital ... taxes and the need for a level playing field for domestic and international investors are very important,” he said. “But many investors are already in the UK, which is a large, deep and transparent market, so we would remain positive while looking at the consultation carefully.” Ferguson-Davie said the wider economic benefits of attracting large-scale investment should be part of the government's calculations, rather than focusing solely on the tax revenue generated. He said the string of regulatory or tax burdens added to the private rental sector over the last few budgets show the danger in the government’s thinking. “You can understand the political motivation, but it has already led to a lot of sales and exits from the market,” Ferguson-Davie said. “I'm not sure it's all necessarily ending up benefiting the renter.” Instead, supply and development have both fallen, and that pushes rents up. He said the new budget will encourage the sale of buy-to-lets, which could benefit the institutional build-to-rent sector — but it doesn’t actually solve any problems. “What the BTR community needs, indeed the housing sector needs, is more incentives to help bring down the cost of development,” he said. “If we're going to have a meaningful change in terms of new houses delivered for sale and for rent, we need the regulatory and tax burden reduced, because otherwise it's just going to get worse.” BTR construction starts have fallen 63% in the last year, with only 4,696 groundbreakings in September, versus 12,674 the year prior, according to Savills data for RE:UK . “Investors needed more than a pause in policy changes,” Kelly said. The budget's business rates package provided more immediate support for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. However, Kelly said the chancellor again failed to deliver meaningful long-term reform. While the absence of another proposed surcharge on higher-value commercial property was welcome, RE:UK has called for the existing surcharge to be repealed and the tax system changed to make investment and refurbishment more attractive. Unsplash/Daniel Bond markets remained stable after the "breathing space" budget. The budget’s impact on London will be mixed, Knight Frank partner and Head of London Research Shabab Qadar said in a statement. The temporary increase in the bank surcharge could dampen a tenant pool that drives London’s global competitiveness, he said.
