items.title: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q
items.description: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published October 29, 2026, 7:27 p.m. EDT | Updated October 29, 2026, 8:21 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Pennymac posted its lowest mortgage origination and acquisition volume since the first quarter of 2024. Supporting Data: While the company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, its servicing pretax income rose to $99 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. PennyMac Financial Services is making deeper cost cuts after its originations fell 30% this summer. The lender and servicer will slash $160 million in annualized operating expenses in the coming months as it anticipates higher-for-longer rates, it said Thursday. That expands on cuts that began this summer in response to some of the worst mortgage market conditions this decade. Processing Content While the company remained well in the black for the third quarter, its combined origination segment volume of $24.4 billion was its lowest mark since the first quarter of 2024. Chairman and CEO David Spector, in an earnings call Thursday evening, described the current landscape as "one of the most constrained origination environments our industry has seen since 2023." Pennymac didn't provide additional details about staff reductions . For the third quarter, Pennymac posted a $29 million profit, surpassing the $22 million net income in the second quarter. That was still a fraction of the $181.5 million profit Pennymac posted at the same time last year. Although elevated rates and heightened competition battered origination performance, the company highlighted stronger income in servicing, and green shoots in artificial intelligence advancements. Inside the numbers The company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, after marks of $38 million and $122.9 million in the prior quarter and year-ago periods, respectively. Servicing pretax income meanwhile rose to $99 million, soaring from $22 million in the second quarter but falling from $157 million a year ago. Pennymac also agreed to sell $29 billion in unpaid principal balance of low-rate conventional mortgage servicing rights, it said. It plans to redeploy the $490 million in proceeds to reduce higher-cost debt, and repurchase common shares. The servicing book ended the quarter slightly up around $737 billion. Revenues fell to end the period at $469 million, declines of 6% quarterly and 26% annually. Executive outlook Company leaders expanded on origination trends, with Pennymac posting greater consumer direct margins with more closed-end second lien volume. Spector also suggested competitive pressures from the government-sponsored enterprises' cash window for smaller brokerages, and the industry leaders' aggressive pricing. "We're picking and choosing our spots, and maintaining market share, and not really getting too caught up in market share at levels that are just not sustainable or that one can rationalize," said Spector. Pennymac also touted its AI advancements, noting that its tech spending is coming down. The lender has 22 proprietary AI agents live in production and is developing 17 more, while its proprietary AI voice agent supported over 1,600 rate locks in the third quarter. "This will allow us to maintain lean operation in today's constrained environment, while ensuring substantial operating leverage when origination volumes normalize," Spector said of the company's AI prowess. What's ahead The firm also announced some executive moves, as President and Chief Mortgage Banking Officer Doug Jones will retire next June. Chief Strategy Officer Kevin Ryan will be elevated to chief financial officer in January, while current CFO Daniel Perotti will remain in that role through the end of the year. Pennymac's Cenlar deal, which will bring its servicing book past $1 trillion , is now expected to close early next year, as executives said they're waiting on one remaining state approval. items.title: Housing Week Ahead: Monthly Trends Data, Mortgage Rates, and Jobs Report
items.description: With all eyes on Election Day , this marks a relatively light week for new Realtor.com economics research reports and housing market indicators. On Wednesday, I'll be issuing our October monthly housing trends report, taking a look at whether elevated mortgage rates caused buyers or sellers to pull back more, as well as what happened to inventory , asking prices, and contract signings. The September snapshot showed a housing market softening under the weight of rising mortgage rates. Median list prices fell, while inventory and price cuts rose. I expect more of the same from the October data, after mortgage rates hit their highest levels since 2023. On Thursday, senior economist Joel Berner will issue our Realtor.com weekly listing data update. As well, senior economist Hannah Jones will have commentary on Freddie Mac's latest mortgage rate reading on Thursday. It’s too early to call the direction of rates this week. But I’ll be watching the bond market, especially the 10-year Treasury yield, for any reaction to the midterms, new developments in the Middle East, and any Fed signals about a December hike. Rates matter locally, too. For buyers in Phoenix; Tucson, AZ; Raleigh, NC; Charlotte, NC; and Louisville, KY, Nov. 1–7 is your best time to buy. If rates ease for a third week in a row, buyers there and elsewhere could have more purchasing power than a month ago, more homes to choose from than a year ago, and fewer buyers to compete with. That’s a winning combination heading into the slow season. One final indicator: I’ll be up bright and early on Friday morning to track the latest labor market data, which covers October unemployment and job growth. September's jobs report was disappointing but not a disaster, adding just 29,000 jobs while unemployment rose to 4.2%. We expect the low-hire, low-fire labor market to continue, which keeps the Federal Reserve focused on inflation ahead of its December meeting. items.title: 3 new apartment projects open their doors
items.description: 3 new apartment projects open their doors Pennrose, Hillpointe and other multifamily developers recently cut ribbons on new buildings in Connecticut, Georgia and Virginia. Published Nov. 2, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Atlantic Boulevard Apartments in Sterling, Va. Retrieved from Atlantic Boulevard Apartments on October 30, 2026 Listen to the article 4 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Although apartment deliveries are slowing down , new projects are still coming online. At the end of October, Washington, D.C.-area developers Green Street Housing and Good Housing opened an attainable development in Virginia, while Pennrose and The Cloud Co. welcomed the first phase of a mixed-use, transit-oriented development in Connecticut. Florida-based Hillpointe, which specializes in attainable multifamily housing, opened its third housing development in Georgia this year. Here is more detail about the three projects that opened last week. Atlantic Boulevard Apartments in Sterling, Virginia Green Street Housing and Good Housing celebrated the opening of Atlantic Boulevard Apartments on Wednesday, which brings 80 units of attainable housing to Sterling, Virginia, according to an Oct. 28 press release. The one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments are designated for those earning up to 60% of Area Median Income. The $31.4 million project does not include any market-rate units or retail and was not mandated by inclusionary zoning, “making it the first 100% attainable new development in Loudoun County in decades,” per the release. Atlantic Boulevard was re-zoned, permitted and built in less than three years through the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors’ expedited review process, per the release. The county’s Fast-Track Commercial Incentive Program targets commercial developments, but the board decided to pilot the Atlantic Boulevard project because of its “unique commitment to attainable housing.” The project was funded through Low Income Housing Tax Credits and Tax-Exempt Bonds from Virginia Housing, an equity investment by Cinnaire and a loan from the county’s Attainable Housing Loan Program. Its amenities include covered bicycle storage, a community room, an exercise room, a tot lot and an outdoor play area alongside resident services programming. Platform at Naugatuck in Naugatuck, Connecticut Optional Caption Courtesy of Pennrose Pennrose, The Cloud Co. and the Borough of Naugatuck hosted a ribbon-cutting for Platform at Naugatuck on Tuesday, according to a press release shared with Multifamily Dive. The new housing represents the first phase of a three-phase project that will ultimately transform a vacant 7-acre site into a mixed-income, mixed-use, transit-oriented community with 180 new apartments across three buildings. The design calls for public green space with a market plaza, a central lawn and gardens “to foster community gathering and shared local experiences,” per the release. The new building brings 60 brand-new apartments and roughly 3,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial space to downtown Naugatuck. It has one- and two-bedroom units for residents earning 30%, 50% and 80% of the AMI as well as market-rate options. Indoor and outdoor amenity spaces include a lounge, a fitness center and a roof deck. The project was financed through LIHTC with construction loans from M&T Bank and Ion Bank, and a permanent loan from the state’s Housing Finance Agency. Connecticut supplied additional funding from various state programs, and the Federal Home Loan Bank of Boston and the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York also provided support. Pointe Grand Cassville in White, Georgia Optional Caption Courtesy of Hillpointe Hillpointe celebrated the opening of Pointe Grand Cassville, a garden-style workforce housing development with 312 units in the Atlanta metro area, according to an Oct. 26 press release shared with Multifamily Dive. It marks Hillpointe’s third attainable development to open in Georgia this year as the firm focuses on building workforce housing in growing markets in the Southeast and beyond. “Northwest Georgia is growing, and attainable housing must keep pace,” Steven Campisi, managing partner and co-founder of Hillpointe, said in the release. “Pointe Grand Cassville adds newly built homes to Atlanta’s suburban and exurban markets, where growth is driving demand. Pointe Grand Cassville offers two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartments with full-size washers and dryers, smart home technology and a covered deck or patio. The open-concept units also feature quartz countertops and stainless steel appliances. Building amenities include a resort-style swimming pool with private cabanas, pickleball courts, a 24-hour fitness center, a clubhouse with a coffee and tea bar, a business center, an outdoor grilling pavilion, a fire pit, a bark park and pet spa, valet trash service, Wi-Fi and EV charging stations. items.title: Houston’s Historic Kirby Mansion Is Demolished To Make Way for Convenience Store
items.description: Preservationists in Houston are up in arms after a historic mansion dating back to 1894 was demolished to erect a convenience store. On Friday, demolition on Kirby Mansion began but was quickly halted by Houston Public Works after it was discovered that a demolition permit had been applied for but not approved. Dozens of locals held a candlelight vigil on Sunday to protest the demolition, but the permit was approved over the weekend. Demolition resumed and was completed on Monday morning. The Kirby Mansion was named after lumber baron and industrialist John Henry Kirby who purchased the small home that was originally on the site in 1896 and expanded it into a 36-room Tudor Revival mansion. Among the many unique features of the home was a library with hidden panels and a “thunder room”—a sound-insulated room built because Kirby's wife, Lelia, had a severe fear of thunderstorms. Loading... After demolition was halted last Friday, part of the mansion's facade remained standing. Houston Chronicle via Getty Images The Kirby family sold the property in 1947, and the mansion served as the headquarters for the Houston-Harris County Red Cross for 30 years, though it had not been occupied in recent years. Over its 132-year history, the mansion hosted presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt , Herbert Hoover , and George H.W. Bush , as well as British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher . This past September, OB Texas Properties LLC, a company owned by Omair Bashir , purchased the property for more than $9.3 million. Bashir and his brother, Usman , are the owners of Brake Time Corner Market, a fast-growing convenience store and gas station chain. In September 2025, Brake Time announced it would be opening 35 new convenience stores across Texas, Arizona , Arkansas , Colorado , and Kansas through the end of 2026, with three planned for Houston. This past June, OB Texas Properties filed a plan for a 13,254-square-foot, one-story commercial building at an address within the mansion’s property boundaries. The filings included a hemp registration—indicating consumable hemp products would also be sold at the location. Local preservationists had rallied to save the mansion, but because it lacked local, state, or federal historic designation, there was little they could do. Loading... In 2018, the property was purchased with the intention of demolishing it and turning it into a car dealership, though those plans never came to fruition. Houston Chronicle via Getty Images Loading... An glimpse into the interior of the demolished mansion shows books still on the shelves in the library. Houston Chronicle via Getty Images Over the weekend, Preservation Houston tried to contact Bashir’s company about removing some of the historic details from the site, including the mansion’s hand-carved oak staircase and imported tiles, but received no response. “We wish the owner had been transparent and honest about the plans for this property and willing to discuss preservation options,” Jennifer Kapral , the executive director of Preservation Houston told Realtor.com in a statement. “We offered to explore ways to give this building a future. We also asked for the opportunity to document it and discuss salvaging irreplaceable materials if demolition went ahead. We received no response. Houston deserves better than this.” “What’s so sad is the people that did buy this, and again, it’s their private property they can do with it as they choose. It just seems like not the best place for a vape store and gas station when there are numerous gas stations within a three-mile radius,” local resident Jason Fuller told the Houston Chronicle . This isn’t the first time the Kirby Mansion was scheduled for demolition. In 2018 Central Houston Auto Properties LLC purchased the property, with the intention of turning it into a car dealership, though those plans never came to fruition. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. items.title: Turning MLS information into value for your clients
items.description: Turning MLS information into value for your clients by Chanel Raesis November 02, 2026 Chanel Raesis is the HAR MLS advisory group chair. Think about how much real estate information your clients can find before they ever call you. They can scroll through listings, check home values, calculate mortgage payments, look at market statistics and now even ask AI what’s happening in the housing market. There’s no shortage of information. But knowing what to do with all that information? That’s a different story. That’s where the Houston Association of REALTORS® ’ MLS and Realtor expertise come together. The MLS gives agents reliable, local market data. As an agent, you help your clients understand what that data actually means for them. And that’s where the real value begins. The numbers don’t tell the whole story We have an incredible amount of information available through the MLS. But our clients usually aren’t looking for more numbers. They’re trying to answer much more personal questions. Can I afford to wait? Do I have room to negotiate? Is my home priced right? Should I make an offer now or keep looking? Take inventory, for example. We can tell a client whether there are more homes on the market, but that alone doesn’t answer the question they really care about: What does that mean for me? For a buyer, more inventory could mean more choices or more negotiating room. For a seller, it could mean facing more competition. And even then, the answer can be different depending on the neighborhood, price range or type of property. That’s one of the things we know so well in real estate: the market is local. A headline about the Houston market may not tell your client what’s happening in the neighborhood where they want to buy or sell. That’s why being able to dig into MLS data and pair it with your own experience is so important. The numbers tell part of the story. The information available to you reaches well beyond one neighborhood or one set of listings. HAR’s data-sharing relationships have expanded the market information available in the MLS, giving subscribers a broader view when clients are looking outside the greater Houston area. So, what about AI? AI is giving all of us new ways to find and use information, and I think there are plenty of opportunities for Realtors to use it as a helpful tool. But it’s just that: a tool. AI doesn’t know your client the way you do. It doesn’t know that your buyer would happily give up an extra bedroom to cut 20 minutes off their commute. It doesn’t know that your seller just accepted a new job and needs to move sooner than expected. You know those things because you’ve had the conversations. You’ve listened. You understand what really matters to them. That human connection is incredibly important, especially when someone is making a decision as personal and significant as buying or selling a home. Making the information useful This is where I believe Realtors have a real opportunity. Instead of simply telling clients what the market is doing, we can help them understand what it means for their next decision. HAR offers tools that can help you put that information to work. MarketInsight can help you keep clients informed about activity and trends in the markets that matter to them, while MLS statistical reports and CMA tools can help you take a closer look at what’s happening in a specific area. The goal isn’t to overwhelm clients with more numbers. It’s to use the right information to have a better conversation. The value is in the context Technology will keep changing. Our clients will continue finding new ways to search for homes, research the market and get answers to their questions. I see that as an opportunity for our profession. Our value has never been about simply having information that no one else can access. It’s about knowing the market, understanding our clients and helping them make sense of the information in front of them. HAR’s MLS gives you the data. You bring the context, experience and personal understanding that turn that data into something meaningful. At the end of the day, clients don’t just need more information. They need someone they trust to help them make a confident decision — and that is where Realtors continue to bring tremendous value. Chanel Raesis is the HAR MLS advisory group chair. items.title: Stay top of mind this holiday season with email, not ad spend
items.description: Stay top of mind this holiday season with email, not ad spend by Marki Lemons-Ryhal November 02, 2026 The holidays do not slow your clients down. They slow your competitors down. Most agents go quietly from Thanksgiving to New Year’s, while the agents with a plan show up in the inbox with something useful. Your email list is the one asset you own outright, and Q4 is when it pays. Why this matters to your GCI I have lived this. I once sent eight emails over nine days to a list of 13,000 contacts and earned $128,635. On the final day, I sent three emails and made more than $40,000. I was nervous. About 1% of the list unsubscribed, roughly 130 people. I let go of 130 people who were never going to buy, and I earned $40,000. I make that trade every time. Build a calendar, not a blast Most agents email when they have a new listing. Top of mind takes rhythm. At a bare minimum, send 36 emails per year, which is three per month. I send 56 annually: two per month tied to my podcast, plus eight for every quarterly webinar. Build your holiday run now: one email in late October, two in November, two in December and one in January. Every email carries an item of value. Never send a plug with nothing inside. Open with their needs, not yours Your first holiday email should show your list you are listening. Send a two-question survey. What is the biggest home task on your winter list? What would you like me to cover in January? Do not make it about you. Make it 100% about the needs of the people on your list. Their answers become your next three emails, so you never stare at a blank screen: one survey, three topics, zero guesswork. Give something worth opening An item of value is something your reader uses in five minutes. Try a winterizing checklist, a list of documents to gather for your tax professional, or a one-page guide to year-end home maintenance. Keep any community event lists general and open to everyone. That protects you under Fair Housing. My son Skyler, an NAR 30 Under 30 honoree, is closing out this year at roughly $200,000 in gross closed income with no ad spend. His item of value is down payment resources. Pick one problem your database has, and be the solution to it. Record once, send everywhere One video is three assets. The MP4 gives you video, the MP3 gives you audio and the transcript gives you text. Hand that transcript to AI, and it drafts your email, landing page and blog post. Your list does not all learn the same way. Use a large, bold font; skip thin, cursive lines; and add audio instructions. Skyler adds roughly 1,700+ contacts a year using faceless videos on Instagram connected to ManyChat. You do not need to be on camera to start. Tag every click In your CRM, tag people when they download or make a purchase, and remove the old tags as they move forward. A seller who grabs your winterizing checklist gets a different follow-up than a buyer who grabs your down payment guide. Email lands harder when it matches where the client is in the process. Read before you send AI is my business partner, but I read every word. Real estate is regulated. Fair Housing rules, license law and the REALTORS® Code of Ethics are your responsibility, not the software’s. Do this before your next showing Pick one problem your clients face this winter, and use Claude to create your item of value. Record a 60-second video explaining the solution, whether your face is in it or not. Paste the transcript into AI and ask for a short email, then read every word for compliance. Build a simple landing page inside of your CRM that delivers the item in exchange for an email address. Schedule six holiday emails now, and send three on the final day of your last campaign. items.title: The power of showing up: Why consistency, connection and community still win in real estate
items.description: The power of showing up: Why consistency, connection and community still win in real estate by Maggie Antillon-Mathews November 02, 2026 When I started my real estate career 25 years ago, things looked very different. There was no Instagram, Facebook, TikTok or artificial intelligence to help generate leads or create marketing campaigns. I didn’t have thousands of online followers or a database filled with automated reminders. I had my business cards, my relationships and a willingness to show up. I attended events, introduced myself to people, followed up and built connections one conversation at a time. I learned that people weren’t necessarily doing business with the agent who had the biggest advertisement. They were doing business with someone they knew, liked and trusted. Twenty-five years later, I find myself reminding agents of those same lessons. Because sometimes, moving forward means going back to the basics. Being visible is not the same as being connected Today, agents have more tools and opportunities to market themselves than ever before. Yet many are struggling to build meaningful relationships. We spend hours creating content, watching engagement and trying to figure out the next marketing trend. But here’s a question I often ask agents: How many actual conversations did you have today? Not likes. Not comments. Not views. Conversations. Technology has made it easier to reach people, but reaching someone and connecting with someone are two very different things. A social media post may remind s omeone you’re in real estate. A personal conversation reminds them why they should trust you. Both have value, but one should never replace the other. Consistency creates opportunity Over the years, I’ve learned that success rarely comes from one big moment. More often, it’s the result of small actions repeated consistently. Making the phone call. Attending the networking event. Following up with someone you met months ago. Checking in with a past client. Offering guidance without expecting anything in return. One of the biggest challenges I see among agents is inconsistency. When business is good, they become consumed with transactions and stop nurturing relationships. When business slows, they scramble to find new opportunities. Imagine what would happen if we treated relationship-building as a daily responsibility rather than something we do only when we need business. Community is your competitive advantage Real estate has always been rooted in community. Before people trust you with one of the biggest financial decisions of their lives, they often want to know who you are, what you stand for and whether you’ll be there when they need you. Get involved. Support local businesses. Volunteer. Attend community events. Build relationships with other professionals. And don’t underestimate the importance of relationships within our own industry. As a managing broker and mentor, I’ve seen how collaboration, education and genuine support can transform an agent’s career. When we share knowledge and help others grow, we create an environment where success isn’t limited to one person. There’s room for all of us to succeed. Embrace technology, but don’t lose yourself in it I’m not suggesting we abandon technology. Quite the opposite. We should use every tool available to become more efficient, better informed and more responsive to our clients. Use your CRM to remember important dates. Use AI to streamline your marketing. Use social media to educate and stay visible. But don’t confuse activity with productivity. Posting five times a day means little if you’re not building relationships or creating opportunities. The goal isn’t to be everywhere. It’s to be remembered by the people who matter. The basics never stopped working I’ve seen markets rise and fall, technology transform our business, and countless trends come and go. But the one thing that hasn’t changed is the importance of human connection. As we prepare for another year, my challenge to agents is simple: Return to the fundamentals. You don’t need to reinvent yourself every time the market changes. Sometimes, you simply need to reconnect with what made this business work in the first place. Today, I have more tools, more experience and more opportunities, but the foundation remains exactly the same. And that’s a lesson worth remembering. Maggie Antillon-Mathews is an award-winning Realtor, senior managing broker at Realty of America, coach, author and mentor with 25 years of experience in the real estate industry. items.title: Your MLS is leveling up (and so can your marketing)
items.description: Your MLS is leveling up (and so can your marketing) by Christy Walker November 02, 2026 Christy Walker is a member of the ARMLS Board of Directors and broker/owner of REMAX Signature. Let's be real. Most of us don't wake up excited about our MLS. We get excited about a new listing, a happy buyer or a closing that finally crossed the finish line. But behind nearly every one of those wins is the data that made it possible. Serving on the Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service Board of Directors has given me a front-row seat to some big changes this year and made me even more aware of just how important this tool is that most of us take for granted. Here's what's happening and why it matters for how you market yourself and your listings. Cooperation is our superpower At the Council of Multiple Listing Services Open House, one idea kept coming up session after session: Cooperation and complete data are the MLS's superpowers. Think about what that means. Competitors agree to share their listings in one trusted place. Each listing gets in front of every buyer with each seller getting maximum exposure. No one else has built a dataset like it. That cooperation is also what makes modern marketing possible. The evolution of IDX lets brokers display each other's listings on their own websites. Today, IDX feeds and syndication send one listing to thousands of websites, portals and apps within minutes. One speaker pointed out that MLS syndication has saved agents millions of dollars. Instead of paying individually to market on websites, major search sites deliver our listings to thousands of buyers daily. However, we have a responsibility to protect that data to ensure listing agents get credit, others aren't profiting unfairly off of our work and the data remains clean. Most consumers have no idea what the MLS does for them, and we're the best people to tell that story. Every time you show a seller how far their listing will travel, you're making the case for cooperation and marketing your value. A new way to lead This spring, ARMLS approved a change to an independent board model. Instead of a large board of practicing Arizona agents, ARMLS is now guided by a smaller board of independent directors who aren't competing in our market. Think of it as a professional board full of experts in finance, law and business strategy. Why does that matter? Our industry is under a legal microscope. When the people setting MLS policy are also competing for the same clients, even the appearance of a conflict creates risk. An independent board removes that perception, protects the MLS (and every one of us who relies on it) and frees ARMLS to make objective, forward-thinking decisions. ARMLS is leading the way and the talk of the MLS industry right now. Agents haven't lost their voice — a shareholder advisory council of agents keeps real-world insight at the table. Independence plus practitioner wisdom is a powerful combination. Three new tools worth your attention Property Shield. Listing fraud is real and growing. Scammers copy legitimate listings, repost them as fake rentals or sales and take deposits from unsuspecting consumers. Property Shield now monitors the web for duplicate and fraudulent copies of listings, alerts agents and helps confirm IDX websites are displaying listing data correctly. It's included at no extra cost to protect your legitimate marketing efforts. Down Payment Resource. Launching Oct. 14 inside Flexmls, DPR connects eligible buyers and listings with down payment assistance and homeownership programs. For first-time buyers who think owning a home is out of reach, that's a game changer and makes you look like a rock star as you provide info on programs that could save your client tons of money or market listings to a new audience. Flexmls Pro app upgrades. The latest iOS update puts more power in your pocket. You can now search within a radius of an address, import contacts from your phone, swipe to compare listings at a glance and search any listing report by keyword, like "HOA." Perfect for those of us who run our business from our car. How smart agents use MLS data in their marketing Now for the fun part: The best marketers I know treat MLS data like a secret ingredient. A few ideas to borrow: Go hyperlocal. Use RapidStats and the monthly ARMLS STAT report to create neighborhood market updates for your social channels. Opinions are easy to scroll past. Real numbers stop the thumb. They even have an infographic you can copy easily if you aren't too techy! Lead with value. Cloud CMA helps you create polished CMAs and buyer tour packets that make you look like the pro you are. Show sellers the reach. In your listing presentation, explain how one MLS entry syndicates to thousands of sites. Sellers love knowing how much their home will be seen. Prospect with purpose. CurbView's public records and mapping can help you build a smarter farm and spot opportunities before your competition. Open doors for buyers. Once DPR launches, highlight that a listing may be eligible for assistance programs. It widens your buyer pool and helps more families say yes. Keep it honest. Since June, ARMLS requires a "Digitally Altered" watermark on virtually staged or edited photos, with the original photo placed right beside it. Beautiful marketing is great. Truthful marketing builds trust that lasts. Protect your brand. Watch for Property Shield alerts so a scammer never gets to market your listing for you. The bottom line Data is only as valuable as the trust behind it. A cooperative marketplace, accuracy, honest marketing and protected consumers make all of us look good. That's the kind of industry I want to be part of, and I'm sure you do too. Your MLS is working hard for you. Put it to work in your marketing! Christy Walker is a member of the ARMLS Board of Directors and broker/owner of REMAX Signature, with offices in Phoenix, Gilbert and Green Valley.
